task:
A collaborator ran a label-free quantitative proteomics experiment comparing 6 treated and 6 control samples (processed in two batches, each containing 3 treated and 3 control samples). The protein-level output of the search software is in data/protein_intensities.tsv: one row per protein group, raw (linear-scale) intensities in the columns named `Intensity <sample>`, empty cells where a protein was not quantified in a sample, plus the columns `Reverse` and `Potential contaminant` (a '+' marks a flagged row). Sample metadata (condition, batch) are in data/samples.tsv; batch is a known nuisance variable.

Identify the proteins that differ in abundance between treated and control, controlling the false discovery rate at 5% with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure across all proteins you test. Do not report reverse-database hits or potential contaminants. Only proteins with at least 3 valid (non-missing) intensity values in each condition are eligible to be reported. Direction of change does not matter; report a protein if it is significantly different in either direction.

Return EXACTLY:

<EVAL_ANSWER>
{"differentially_abundant_proteins": ["<Protein IDs value>", ...]}
</EVAL_ANSWER>

where each list item is the value in the `Protein IDs` column.
design_source: Label-free proteomics missing values are largely missing-not-at-random (low-abundance proteins drop out) and per-sample loading differs; naive min/zero imputation plus t-test manufactures false positives (Lazar et al. 2016, J Proteome Res 15:1116).
